Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 244 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2018-19) 
 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 244 is located in central Alberta. The unit is adjacent to the border of 
Saskatchewan and is approximately 919 km2. The habitat is dominated by agricultural land (pasture and cropland) 
interspersed with parkland vegetation.  
Previous aerial ungulate surveys conducted in these units have used the strip transect s urvey method and were 
conducted. No previous white-tailed deer, mule deer, or moose estimates exist as this Unit has no history having 
been surveyed in previous years.

Survey Method 
From January 9 to 11, 2019, a strip transect survey of WMU 244 was conducted flying east-west lines at 1.6 
kilometre (1 mile) intervals resulting in a 25% coverage (with 400 metre wide survey strip). Snow conditions were 
good. At each observation point, ungulates were counted by species, and when possible, classified by sex and 
age. Bucks were also classified by antler size as ‘small’ (spike or two points on one or both antlers), ‘medium’ 
(antlers with 3 or more points; antlers inside ears) or large (antlers with ≥ 4 points, antlers outside of ears).  
 
Because transects varied in length (see Krebs 2014, Jolly 1969), we calculated the average density (R; #/km2) of 
mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose by summing the total animals counted per transect (∑x) by total area 
searched (length of transects multiplied by 400 m survey strip [∑z]). For a population estimate (unequal sized units, 
sampling without replacement), we multiplied the average density (R) by the overall area of the WM U (Z). A 
correction factor for detectability (estimated at 83%; Habib et al. 2012) can be applied to WTDE and MUDE density 
and population estimates in the Parkland for strip widths of 400 metres. A correction factor of 95% was applied for 
moose population estimates. We calculated the width of the 90% confidence interval by multiplying the t statistic 
for the left-tailed inverse of the Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without replacement) of 
the abundance estimate where SE=sq root variance, and variance=N*(N-n)/(n*(n-1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-2*R*∑xz) with N 
as the total number of possible transects given 100% coverage, and n as the number of transects sampled.  Due to 
the variation in transect lengths, population estimates were determined by Jolly’s (1969) method for sampling 
unequal sized units without replacement (Krebs 2014). 
 
Because of the timing of this survey some antler drop is expected to have happened, resulting in a male -skewed 
unclassified portion of the population, in particular for mule and white-tailed deer.  
 
Results 
Out of 84 possible transects, a total of 21 transects were surveyed for a total effort of 230 km2. Non-ungulate 
species observed during the survey included coyotes, porcupines, red fox, and snowy owls.  
There were 225 white-tailed deer observed within 47 groups. Of the 225 white-tailed deer observed:  
 
 51 (20%) were bucks 
 127 (50%) were does 
 71 (28%) were fawns 
 6 (2%) were not classified 
 
Of the 51 bucks identified, 11 (22%) were classified as small, 14 (27%) medium, 6 (12%) large, and 20 (39%) were 
unclassified. The buck:doe ratio was 0.40 and the fawn:doe ratio was 0.56 (Table 1). The average white-tailed deer 
density was estimated at 1.30 individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate of 1194 individuals (Table 
1). This corresponds to a white-tailed deer population split estimate of 245 bucks, 609 does and 341 fawns. 
 
There were 47 mule deer observed within 7 groups. Of the 47 mule deer identified:  
 
 12 (26%) were bucks 
 17 (60%) were does 
 13 (28%) were fawns 
 5 (11%) were not classified 
 
Of the 12 bucks observed, 3 (25%) were classified as small, 1 (8%) medium, 1 (8%) large and 7 (58%) were not 
classified. The buck:doe ratio was 0.71 and the fawn:doe ratio was 0.76 (Table 2). The average mule deer density 
was estimated at 0.24 individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate of 220 individuals (Table 2). This 
corresponds to a mule deer population split estimate of 63 bucks, 89 does and 68 fawns.

There were 15 moose observed within 10 groups. Of the 15 moose identified: 
 3 (20%) were bulls 
 9 (60%) were cows 
 3 (20%) were calves 
 0 (%) were not classified 
The bull:cow ratio was 0.33 and the calf:cow ratio was 0.33 (Table 3). The average moose density was estimated 
at 0.07 individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate of 63 (Table 3) and corresponds to moose 
population split estimate of 13 bulls, 38 cows and 13 calves.  
Lastly, there were 0 elk (both on and off transect) observed in the WMU.
